title: Ingestion architectures: indexer, push, event-driven, batch
summary: Four ways to get content into a search index: a managed indexer pulls on a schedule, your code pushes documents, an event pipeline reacts to changes, or a batch job rebuilds in bulk.
useIf: You must pick how content reaches the index and can state the freshness target, the source type and who will operate the pipeline.
avoidIf: You treat the choice as permanent: most real systems mix a pull path for bulk content with a push path for hot content.

explain.md: **Pull** means an indexer connects to a supported data source, detects what changed and can run a skillset (chunk, embed, OCR) on the way in [[tr1]]. You declare it and Azure AI Search runs it. The smallest schedule interval is 5 minutes and the longest is 1,440 minutes [[tr3]], and you should plan for runs that stop at about 2 hours [[tr31]].

**Push** means your code calls the Index Documents API with the actions `upload`, `merge`, `mergeOrUpload` and `delete`. A request carries at most 1,000 documents or 16 MB, and HTTP 207 means some documents failed while 503 means wait and retry [[tr2]]. You own parsing, chunking and embedding, which is the price of full control.

**Event-driven** is push with a trigger. A blob event, a Cosmos DB change feed entry or a Debezium record lands on a queue, a worker parses and embeds, then pushes. Event Grid and Debezium both deliver at least once, so the worker must be idempotent [[tr26]] [[tr25]]. **Batch** is a scheduled or one-off job that rebuilds or backfills the whole corpus, and it is the simplest way to re-embed.

explain.title: Four paths into one index
explain.alt: Sources feed an indexer, an event queue with a worker, or a batch job. The worker and the batch job write through the push API. The indexer and the push API both write to the search index.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  S[Sources] --> I[Indexer pull]
  S --> E[Events or CDC]
  E --> Q[Queue]
  Q --> W[Worker]
  W --> P[Push API]
  S --> B[Batch job]
  B --> P
  I --> X[(Search index)]
  P --> X

explain.title: Mix paths on purpose
explain.md: Use the indexer for the long tail of stable files and a push path for the few sources where seconds matter. Both can write to the same index if they agree on the document key (see the idempotency topic).

whereToUse: Indexer: knowledge bases over Blob Storage, ADLS Gen2, OneLake, Azure SQL or Cosmos DB where hourly or daily freshness is fine
Push: SaaS tools, wikis and internal systems that no indexer can read, or content that needs custom parsing
Event-driven: support tickets, chat transcripts or order data that must be searchable within seconds
Batch: first load, backfills and re-embedding after a model change
Foundry IQ knowledge sources, which generate an indexer pipeline for you when your source kind is supported [[tr13]]

use: Pick the indexer when the source is a supported GA store, minutes of staleness are acceptable and built-in skills cover the work
Pick push or event-driven when you need seconds of freshness, custom parsing, dead-letter handling or a source with no indexer
Pick batch when the data changes rarely or you are rebuilding the whole index
Keep the sink idempotent whatever the path, because retries and replays happen
avoid: Do not run an event pipeline for a corpus that changes nightly: you pay for queues, workers and on-call for no freshness gain
Do not use an indexer for a source whose indexer is still preview when you need a production service level
Do not hand-write a push pipeline to chunk and embed files that a skillset already handles
flips: Freshness target drops from hours to seconds: move the hot path from indexer to event-driven push
The source has no indexer or the indexer is preview and you need a firm SLA: push from your own code
The team has no capacity to run queues and workers: accept minutes of staleness and use the indexer

pitfalls.symptom: New files show up much later than the schedule suggests
pitfalls.cause: The schedule is only the minimum interval. A big backlog keeps one run busy until it hits the run time cap
pitfalls.fix: Check run history, split the source, give the hot path to a push pipeline

pitfalls.symptom: Push requests fail with 413 or return 207
pitfalls.cause: A batch above 1,000 documents or 16 MB, or some documents failed validation
pitfalls.fix: Cap batch size, read the per-document status, retry only failed keys and back off on 503

pitfalls.symptom: The same chunk is indexed twice after a retry
pitfalls.cause: Event delivery is at least once and the key was generated per attempt
pitfalls.fix: Derive the key from the source id and chunk position, and use `mergeOrUpload`

scenarios.title: Policies in blob storage, hourly is fine
scenarios.situation: A small team indexes a few thousand PDFs and Word files that live in Blob Storage. Editors change a handful per day. Nobody on the team wants to run extra infrastructure.
constraints: Source is a supported GA store
Staleness of an hour is acceptable
unknowns: Is any document needed within minutes of publishing?
Do files need custom parsing that skills cannot do?
scenarios.question: How do you ingest?

options.name: Scheduled indexer with a skillset
options.why: It matches the source, the freshness and the team size, and built-in change detection handles updates.
options.tradeoff: 5 minute minimum interval and limited control over parsing.

options.name: Event-driven push with Event Grid and a worker
options.why: It adds queues, workers and dead-letter handling to buy seconds nobody asked for.
options.tradeoff: Right when freshness is seconds or the parsing is custom.

options.name: Nightly batch rebuild
options.why: Simple and cheap to reason about, and it fits the update rate.
options.tradeoff: Re-embeds unchanged files and stays stale up to a day.

flips.if: Editors need changes searchable within a minute
flips.then: Add an event-driven push path for those folders and keep the indexer for the rest.
Push from your code, since a skillset cannot run it.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the pipeline to the freshness target and the team, not to the most sophisticated option.

scenarios.title: Tickets searchable in seconds
scenarios.situation: Support tickets live in a SaaS tool that can call a webhook on every change. Agents expect a new ticket to be findable within 30 seconds. Volume is high and bursty after incidents.
constraints: A platform team can run queues
unknowns: How large can a burst be?
What happens to a ticket that keeps failing?
scenarios.question: Which architecture fits?

options.name: Webhook to queue to worker to push API
options.why: The queue absorbs bursts, the worker can retry and dead-letter, and push gives seconds of freshness.
options.tradeoff: More moving parts and an idempotent worker are required.

options.name: Scheduled indexer every 5 minutes
options.why: The source has no indexer and the 5 minute floor misses the 30 second target.
options.tradeoff: Right for supported stores where minutes of lag are fine.

options.name: Webhook straight to the push API
options.why: Fewer parts and low latency for light traffic.
options.tradeoff: A burst or a throttled embedding call loses events, with no replay or dead-letter path.

flips.if: Volume is low and a lost event is cheap to repair
flips.then: Direct webhook to push is acceptable.
A scheduled export plus batch push is simpler.

scenarios.takeaway: Seconds of freshness and bursts both argue for a queue in front of the push call.

quiz.q: The business wants new documents searchable within 30 seconds. Which statement about indexers is correct?
options: An indexer can be scheduled every 10 seconds
The smallest indexer schedule interval is 5 minutes, so a push or event path is needed
Indexers push documents faster than the Index Documents API
quiz.explain: The schedule floor is 5 minutes, so seconds of freshness need a push path. Indexers cannot run every 10 seconds. They do not beat push on latency. They can run skillsets, which is a reason to choose them elsewhere.

quiz.q: You must push 4,500 small documents. Each request may carry at most 1,000 documents. What is the minimum number of requests?
quiz.explain: 4,500 divided by 1,000 is 4.5, so you need 5 requests. The 16 MB limit also applies, so check payload size if documents are large.

quiz.q: Which are real reasons to prefer your own push pipeline over an indexer?
options: You need custom parsing the skillset cannot do
You want to avoid writing any code
You need to dead-letter poison documents and replay them
quiz.explain: No indexer, custom parsing and replay control all favour push. Avoiding code is the reason to choose the indexer, so it is not a reason to leave it.

flashcards.front: What are the smallest and largest indexer schedule intervals?
flashcards.back: 5 minutes and 1,440 minutes (24 hours), set as an XSD duration such as `PT2H`.

flashcards.front: Push API batch limits and status codes?
flashcards.back: 1,000 documents or 16 MB per request. 413 is too large, 207 is partial failure, 503 means wait and retry.

flashcards.front: Why must event-driven workers be idempotent?
flashcards.back: Event Grid and Debezium deliver at least once, so the same change can arrive twice. The sink must tolerate replays.
